open_questions: Wikipedia was read to character 100,000 of 168,274; the rest (his death, legacy detail, the later kits) was not read.

The hi-hat: Wikipedia has him drop it from the larger kit of 1966 and reinstate it later, and Far Out says he 'completely excised' it; but the tabs read put a hat on I Can't Explain, Pinball Wizard, Won't Get Fooled Again, 5:15 and Who Are You. Which songs he played without one is not settled.

Two bass drums from about 1966 (the 'Pictures of Lily' kit has two 22-inch); the tabs write one kick line, and Portnoy's 'constant pulsating 8th notes on the kick drums' are not visible in them. Where the second bass drum is heard is unread.
The Modern Drummer Hall of Fame piece (2003) was read only in the excerpt online; Mark Kelso's comments on playing Tommy are cut off.
Rolling Stone's 2016 entry on him (no. 2) was not read; only its placing.
Beat placement: nothing measured. Entwistle says he sped up and slowed down by mood; Astley that he kept time all the same.
Live at Leeds (1970) and the 1969-70 live recordings, where the double bass drums are said to be most audible, were not read or transcribed.

identity.name: Keith Moon

born.place: Central Middlesex Hospital, Wembley, Middlesex, England

home_scenes: the London mod and R&B scene (the Who, from 1964)
identity.summary: The Who's drummer from 1964 to his death in 1978, from I Can't Explain and My Generation through Tommy, Who's Next and Quadrophenia to Who Are You. Taught by Carlo Little and in love with Gene Krupa, surf music and Motown, he played the drums as a lead instrument and followed the vocal rather than the bass: tom-toms, crashes and fills 'in places that other people would never have thought of putting them' (Daltrey), two bass drums from about 1966, and no drum solos. Ranked second only to John Bonham by Rolling Stone (2016).

teachers.name: Carlo Little
teachers.what: Lessons at ten shillings each; Little was Screaming Lord Sutch's drummer.

traditions.impact: Gene Krupa was his favourite musician, 'whose flamboyant style he later copied'.

traditions.tradition: American surf music, R&B and Motown
traditions.impact: Surf music and R&B (Hal Blaine as an example), Motown and the Beach Boys; The Kids Are Alright's snare on every beat.

traditions.tradition: British beat and rock and roll drummers
traditions.impact: He admired DJ Fontana, Tony Meehan of the Shadows and Viv Prince of the Pretty Things.

formative_events.event: Joined the Sea Cadet Corps band on the bugle, found it too hard and switched to drums.
Left school, became a radio repairman, and bought his first kit with the wages.
Auditioned for the Who in April 1964 in place of Doug Sandom; by the usual account he broke a bass drum pedal and two heads on a borrowed kit and was asked to join.

eras.label: The early Who: maximum R&B
eras.context: Shel Talmy's singles and My Generation: Ludwig, then Premier from late 1965; stops for the vocal, rolls, the snare on every beat.

eras.label: Pictures of Lily and Tommy
eras.context: The double bass drum 'Pictures of Lily' kit; Tommy (1968-69); Woodstock and Live at Leeds.
defining_traits: crashes in the middle of a roll

eras.label: Who's Next and Quadrophenia
eras.context: Playing to Townshend's synthesiser tracks for Glyn Johns: 'more formal and less reliant on long drum fills'; back to his old style on Quadrophenia. Timbales, gongs and timpani on the kit.
defining_traits: a crash ridden as a ride

eras.label: The last years
eras.context: Two Sides of the Moon (1975); Who Are You (1977-78), his playing 'noticeably deteriorated'; the Shepperton film of May 1978.

genres.notes: Who's Next, Live at Leeds, Quadrophenia.
The rock operas, Tommy and Quadrophenia.

evidence.note: No measurement found; Entwistle: he 'tended to play faster or slower according to his mood'.

swing.notes: Straight eighths in every tab read; My Generation's rolls in eighth-note triplets.

dynamics.balance: Loud throughout: crashes, toms and rolls over the time; ghosts only in a few places (Pinball Wizard's chorus, Baba O'Riley's verse).

feel_profile.interaction: Plays to the vocal rather than the bass: 'he always played with the vocals' (Entwistle); he stops and starts with Daltrey in My Generation. Daltrey: 'Pete and John as two knitting needles and Keith was the ball of wool.'

hand_techniques.name: Fills everywhere
hand_techniques.description: Fills inside the phrase as well as at its end, round the toms over the kick in eighths; Daltrey: 'in places that other people would never have thought of putting them'; Portnoy: 'the furious stampede of constant tom fills'.

hand_techniques.name: Crashes in the middle of a roll
hand_techniques.description: A 'steady whirlwind of crash cymbals' (Portnoy); a crash ridden in eighths as a ride (Baba O'Riley's crash 2); Peart liked 'putting crash cymbals in the middle of a roll'.

hand_techniques.name: Eighth-note-triplet rolls
hand_techniques.description: My Generation's rolls on the snare, falling to the floor tom, over the kick on every beat.

hand_techniques.name: Snare threes
hand_techniques.description: Runs of three sixteenths on the snare inside the bar (Won't Get Fooled Again, 5:15).

foot_techniques.name: Two bass drums
foot_techniques.description: With Ginger Baker a pioneer of the double bass drum in rock; the Pictures of Lily kit has two 22-inch; Portnoy hears 'constant pulsating 8th notes on the kick drums'.

foot_techniques.name: The kick in eighths under the fills
foot_techniques.description: The kick on every eighth under fills round the toms (Won't Get Fooled Again, Baba O'Riley).

devices_search.note: None found. Every tab read is in 4/4 bar Substitute's odd 2/4 bars. My Generation's triplets are eighth-note triplets inside a 4/4 fill, not a cross pulse; I Can't Explain's band push in dotted quarters (crashes on 1, the "and" of 2 and 4) lasts one bar and is the band's figure, not a sustained 3:2; Who Are You's half-time verse is a feel, not a metric modulation. Music Must Change in 6/8 is the one song he could not play (Wikipedia, Who Are You). Nothing read names a polyrhythm, an odd meter or a metric modulation in his playing.

voice_language.snare: 2 and 4 on most songs, every beat on The Kids Are Alright, 3 alone in Who Are You's verse; threes, triplet rolls and accents with the crashes.
voice_language.kick: On 1 and 3 and round the riff; eighths under the fills.
voice_language.toms: Everywhere: fills round the rack toms with the kick in eighths, pairs on the floor tom (Pinball Wizard), eighths on the mid tom (The Kids Are Alright's middle).
voice_language.hihat: Eighths, half-open in Won't Get Fooled Again; missing from some kits of 1966-69.
voice_language.cymbals: Crashes on 1, on the "and"s and with the band's pushes; a crash 2 ridden as a ride (Baba O'Riley); the ride in eighths (My Generation, The Kids Are Alright); a china and a gong later.

aesthetic: big, loud kit with many toms
sound_profile.cymbal_character: Zildjian in 1964-65 (Wikipedia); later a gong, and many crashes.

by_era.description: Shel Talmy's tight, trebly IBC and Pye records; Atkins calls the early recordings tinny.
Glyn Johns's big room at Olympic: the kit heard whole, under the synthesiser.

sample_hints.60s: A 1960s kit, ringing toms, thin crashes washing.
sample_hints.70s: Big rock kit played hard in a big room, big crashes.

signature_traits.label: Drums as a lead instrument
signature_traits.description: He played to the vocal, not the bass: 'he always played with the vocals' (Entwistle); Daltrey's ball of wool between two knitting needles.

signature_traits.label: Fills everywhere
signature_traits.description: Tom fills and rolls inside the phrase as well as at its end; 'controlled chaos' (Portnoy).

signature_traits.label: A whirlwind of crashes
signature_traits.description: Crashes on the "and"s and with every push, a crash ridden in eighths (Baba O'Riley).

signature_traits.label: Stops with the vocal
signature_traits.description: My Generation: the band's chord, nothing under Daltrey's line, a pickup into the response.

signature_traits.label: No drum solos
signature_traits.description: He refused to play drum solos in concert: 'Drum solos are boring!' (Madison Square Garden, 1974).

signature_traits.label: Kit destruction
signature_traits.description: Broke a pedal and two heads at his audition; stage destruction part of the Who's act.

patterns.name: I Can't Explain: the verse pair
patterns.function: Eighths on the hat; the snare on 2, its "and" and 4, the kick on 1 and 3; then the kick on the "and" of 3

evidence.note: Songsterr bars 6 and 8 (11 of 13 bars of the first verse).

patterns.name: My Generation: the stop and the ride
patterns.function: The band's chord on 1 and nothing under Daltrey's line, the snare's pickup into the response; then eighths on the ride, the snare on 2 and 4

evidence.note: Songsterr bars 6 and 7, read in sextuplets (the tab's bar 5 is empty; the chord on its 1 is the band's).

patterns.name: My Generation: the triplet rolls
patterns.function: A crash on 1 and 3 over the ride, then a bar of snare in eighth-note triplets over the kick on every beat, the floor tom on 1 and 3

evidence.note: Songsterr bars 41 and 42 (the pair recurs in the last choruses, and as crash and floor-tom bars in the coda).

patterns.name: The Kids Are Alright: Motown on the ride
patterns.function: Eighths on the ride, the snare on every beat, the kick on 1, 2, its "and", 3, 4 and its "and"

evidence.note: Songsterr bar 4.

patterns.name: Pinball Wizard: the verse
patterns.function: Eighths on the hat, a crash on the "and" of 3, the floor tom's pair after 2, the kick on 1, its "and", 3, its "and" and the "and" of 4

evidence.note: Songsterr bars 30-35 (6 of 8); the pair falls between sixteenths in the tab and is written on the "a" of 2 and 3.

patterns.name: Baba O'Riley: the crash 2 in eighths
patterns.function: The crash on 1 and 4 over a crash 2 ridden in eighths, the snare accented on 2 and 4; then the crash 2 alone

evidence.note: Songsterr bars 27 and 28 (the pair x3 in the intro, x4 in the chorus).

patterns.name: Won't Get Fooled Again: the verse
patterns.function: The hat half-open on the eighths from the "and" of 1, a crash 2 on 4, the snare on 2 and 4

evidence.note: Songsterr bar 26; no verse bar repeats in the tab.

patterns.name: 5:15: the horn pushes
patterns.function: Crashes and the kick with the horns on the "and"s of 2 and 4, the hat between, the snare on 2 and 4

evidence.note: Songsterr bar 31.

patterns.name: Who Are You: the half-time verse
patterns.function: Quarters on the hat, the snare on 3 alone, the kick on 1, 2, its "and" and 4

evidence.note: Songsterr bars 38-39 and 42-43.

equipment.label: Premier, red sparkle
equipment.layout_notes: His first Premier kit, from late 1965, with two high toms; Ludwig drums and Zildjian cymbals before it (1964-65).

equipment.label: Premier 'Pictures of Lily'
equipment.layout_notes: Two 22-inch bass drums, three mounted toms, two 16-inch floor toms; reissued by Premier in 2006 as the 'Spirit of Lily'. Tommy was cut on a borrowed double bass drum kit.

equipment.label: Premier, with timbales, gongs and timpani
equipment.layout_notes: From 1970 timbales, gongs and timpani; at Shepperton (May 1978) a chrome kit with a row of rack toms and a gong behind.

affiliations.name: The Who
affiliations.notes: In place of Doug Sandom (1964); Kenney Jones replaced him (November 1978).

evidence.note: Lessons at ten shillings each; Little played with Screaming Lord Sutch.
His favourite musician, 'whose flamboyant style he later copied'.
Surf music and R&B, 'Hal Blaine' given as an example of the style.
Elvis Presley's drummer; one he admired.
The Shadows.
The Pretty Things.
The Who, April 1964.
The Who, November 1978; Townshend: 'one of the few British drummers who could fill Keith's shoes'.
His godson ('Uncle Keith'), to whom he gave a drum kit as a child; the Who's drummer 1996-2025.
A close friend; he told Starr he had 'just been filling in for the last fifteen years'.

philosophy.idea: Do not work a part out too far: the same arrangement every night makes the drummer an automaton.
Build up in different ways each time: on the timpani, on a cymbal, or with a roll round the kit.

innovations: The drums as a lead voice in rock, following the vocal
Two bass drums in rock, with Ginger Baker
Constant fills and crashes as the part itself

accolades.award: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (the Who)
Rolling Stone readers' poll, second-greatest drummer
Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Drummers of All Time, no. 2

cultural_references.description: Ray Davies (1990): 'Keith Moon changed the sound of drumming.'
Moon (Melody Maker, 1970): 'I suppose as a drummer, I'm adequate. I've got no real aspirations to be a great drummer.'

common_misconceptions: That he never kept time: Jon Astley, 'You didn't think he was keeping time, but he was.'
That he never used a hi-hat: the tabs of his records put one on most songs; he dropped it from the 1966 kit and reinstated it later.

beatbreaker.default_kit_sound: A big rock kit in a big room, many toms, crashes washing over it; a ringing 1960s kit for the early songs
generation_rules: Straight eighths, almost no ghost notes, everything loud.
Fills inside the phrase as well as at its end: round the toms over the kick in eighths, snare threes, triplet rolls.
Crashes on 1, on the "and"s and with the band's pushes; a crash ridden as a ride.
Follow the vocal: stop with it, pick up into the response.

lineage_display.lineage_blurb: Krupa's showmanship, Carlo Little's lessons and the surf and Motown records, played as a lead voice; Peart, Collins, Jordison and his godson Zak Starkey after him.
